Project dossier · status 30 Oct 2026 · round 24

Grand Theft
Coconut Creek

A top-down open-city crime and driving game for phones, set in Coconut Creek, Florida. Real 3D in the browser: every building, car, palm tree and person is made by Python scripts in headless Blender. It plays like a pocket Chinatown Wars-style sandbox: drive, crash, get out, run, steal cars, and lose the police. Right now the whole focus is making driving feel good on a phone before any story or quests go in.

  • Live: grand-theft-coconut-creek.vercel.app
  • Platform: iPhone Safari, Android Chrome, portrait
  • Engine: Three.js r170 + headless Blender 5.2
  • Hosting: Vercel, auto-deploy from GitHub
  • Code: Marcsarno/Indie-Games › city-clone
  • Made by: Marc, directing; Claude Code, building

Playable verbs

Drive

Joystick or button controls, handbrake slides, skid marks. Crashes give sparks, shake and sound. Palms and oaks snap and fall when you hit them, and parked cars get shoved.

On foot

Get out anywhere. Walk or run, and punch with combos, hit-stop and knockdowns. Enter any parked car, or pull a driver out of traffic (carjack).

Trouble

Punching, running people over and hard crashes raise heat. Police chase you, ram you, and set roadblocks at 3★. You get “Busted” or “Wasted”, then respawn with a fade.

The world

A stylised Coconut Creek: real road names and landmarks, laid out on an island so the edges make sense. Marc drew the layout as reference maps, and the code traces them.

Roads

  • Lyons Rd is the main north–south spine: 3 lanes each way and a palm median. It goes through every junction.
  • Coconut Creek Pkwy and Wiles Rd run east–west, as in the real city.
  • Traffic lights only at the big crossings. Smaller side streets are right-in / right-out across the median, and small T-junctions are stop signs.
  • An automatic audit flags junctions under 55°, junctions too close together, and dead ends: it went from 27 flags to 1.
  • Bridges with rails are added wherever a road crosses water. Two closed bridges mark the map exits.

Landmarks and districts

  • Publix shopping centre, Seminole Casino Coconut Creek (faces the Parkway so the sign reads), City Hall with a butterfly sculpture, police station, schools and courts.
  • The Promenade at Coconut Creek: an entry arch, shops on both sides, a cinema at the end.
  • Trash Mountain, a landfill you can drive up (a spiral road to the summit), in the NE corner.
  • Neighbourhoods around lakes, apartments, gas stations, industrial and park districts (Windmill Park, Lakeside Park).

Portrait phone, two thumbs. A keyboard works on desktop. Two driving schemes exist today, and Marc picks one in the pause menu.

Camera

Fixed north-up, tilted 45°, 44 m away (Marc’s chosen view). It looks a little ahead of the car and zooms out up to 22% at top speed. The minimap is a circle in the top-right corner, and tapping it opens the full map.

Phone-specific handling

  • No page zoom, no copy/paste popup, no long-press magnifier, no swipe-back while playing. The page never scrolls or bounces.
  • Every control lets go if the app is switched, rotated or loses focus, so nothing stays “held”.
  • Sound plays even with the iPhone ringer switch on silent (iOS 17+).
Marc’s verdict before round 24: the joystick is great while driving forward, but turning around and reversing “just stops”, and after hitting something it “freezes you in place”. Round 24 fixed the reverse-steering bug. The bigger control redesign is the next stage (see What’s next).

Driving physics

A hand-written arcade car with no physics engine, so every number maps to one feel. It agrees with the shape that open-source arcade cars share.

The car model, each physics step

  1. Read input (stick or buttons) and turn it into a steering target and gas, brake or reverse.
  2. Ease the wheel toward the target: 5 per second in, 8 per second back to centre.
  3. Wheel angle shrinks with speed, from 28.6° when slow to 6.9° at top speed.
  4. Split the velocity into forward and sideways along the car’s nose.
  5. Forward: acceleration that fades toward top speed, brakes, handbrake, coasting drag.
  6. Sideways: bled away each step (grip). When sliding, grip drops, so the tail swings.
  7. Turn rate is bicycle-model (speed ÷ wheelbase × tan of the wheel angle), eased in for weight.
  8. Hills: gravity pulls the car down slopes (Trash Mountain).
  9. Collisions (below), then skid marks when sliding.

Physics runs 120 times a second with a fixed step. Since round 24 the car is drawn between the last two steps, so it doesn’t stutter against the 60 Hz screen.

Crashes and contact

  • The car and every obstacle are polygons in 2D, using SAT overlap with an impulse response, bounce and wall friction.
  • “Forgiving” walls: slow bumps don’t bounce, and shallow hits turn the nose along the wall so you slide instead of stopping.
  • Car vs car: your car counts as 2.2× heavier, so you push through traffic. Parked cars come loose and slide, and cops spin.
  • Trees: hit a palm or oak above walking pace and it falls (you keep 80–90% of your speed), sinks away, and regrows when you’re far off.
  • Shrubs, hedges and posts are soft: the car ploughs through, slowed.
  • People: squish, small blood splat, sometimes a tumbling “ragdoll” (Blood can be switched off).
  • Damage is off while testing: crashes cost speed only.
  • An Unstick button appears after 2.5 s of being wedged.

Current numbers vs the research brief’s starting values

Marc researched “what makes driving feel good on a phone” (a 7-report brief). Its values are untested starting points, and nobody has measured “feel”. They are a direction for tuning, not a target.

DialGame nowBrief startWhat it means
Top speed28 m/s (63 mph)26–28Same
Acceleration15 m/s²9Ours is punchier
Brakes34 m/s²16Ours stops from 61 mph in 11.7 m (measured), which is harsh
Steering at 22 mph≈21°13°Ours turns about 1.6× sharper
Steering at 34 mph≈17°8°About 2× sharper, so possibly twitchy
Wheel in / out rate5 / 8 per s5 / 8Same
Turn response (weight)10 per s12Close
Grip8 per s, no cap9 per s, capped at 13 m/s²Ours rarely slides without the handbrake
Stick dead zone0.15, linear0.10, curve 1.4The brief wants a softer centre

Tuning rule adopted from the brief: one dial per round, at most 20% change, logged in TUNING_LOG.md together with the complaint in Marc’s own words.

Game systems

Traffic AI

Cars follow a lane graph built from the road map, driving on the right. They keep distance with a car-following model and stop at red lights. At junctions they take turns, yield to bigger roads, and wait for room on the exit. They pass parked obstacles, and a deadlock breaker keeps jams moving. Cars appear off-screen and vanish behind you.

Pedestrians

People walk both sidewalks, turn corners and cross at junctions. They dodge fast cars, flee or freeze after violence, and panic spreads. Their drivers jump out and run when you carjack them.

Police

Crimes add heat, and heat turns into stars (1–4). Cops path over the road graph, chase directly when close, ram at 2★ and set roadblocks at 3★. Wrecking enough cops drops a star (the Chinatown Wars rule). Stay unseen and stars fade. Get pinned and you’re busted (−10% cash).

Missions (test set)

Publix Run, Casino Shuttle, Trash Mountain Summit, Heat Check. Drive slowly into a yellow beacon to start, then reach the green goal before the timer ends for cash. These are placeholders until quests (Dave) arrive.

Screens and safety

Title screen, pause menu, full map, a controls hint on first play, Wasted/Busted respawn at City Hall or the police station. Autosave every 10 s (cash, missions, car spot). The game recovers if the phone drops the 3D context.

Sound

Synthesised in the browser, with no sound files: an engine with a simple gearbox pitch, tyre squeal, crash thumps, horn, squish and ambience. Sound can be switched off in the menu.

Art and pipeline

No hand modelling and no downloaded assets. Concept images (Marc’s references) become Python scripts that build the models in Blender, run headless in a cloud container.

Marc’s concept art + maps→map data in Python (road points, districts)→headless Blender scripts→glTF + colliders/props/graph JSON→Meshopt compression→Three.js page→GitHub push → Vercel

Vehicles

Rendering on phones

  • Static scenery merged into tiles (draw distance 140 m). Trees and plants are instanced. Only nearby cars cast shadows, with snapped shadows to avoid shimmer.
  • Simple Lambert materials for the city, fog to hide the far edge, and a hidden warm-up draw at load to avoid first-time hitches.
  • Pixel ratio capped at 2, with automatic resolution drop if frames are slow. Every file gets a content hash and a one-year cache.
  • Measured on Marc’s phone: about 60 fps, JS 6 ms, render 3.2 ms, worst frame 38 ms (the warm-up draw was added for that hitch, not yet re-measured).

Testing tools

Test track (round 24)

An empty lot 700 m east of the city, reached from the pause menu. The drills are painted on the ground:

  • 1 straight 250 m + 2 brake box
  • 3 easy slalom (cones 18 m apart), 4 hard slalom (12 m)
  • 5 figure eight, 6 drift circle
  • 7 hairpin, 8 city corner, 9 narrow alley (4 m), 10 wall scrape (10° and 30° walls)

Crossing the start and finish lines prints the time, wall touches, top speed, biggest slide and cones hit.

Tune panel + readout

Every driving number is in one list, in groups with units and safe ranges, and changes apply live. “Copy settings + track results” produces text Marc pastes back into the build chat. The driving readout shows speed, slide angle, steering asked vs got, wall touches and fps.

Measurement HUD (?hud=1)

Frame time percentiles, per-system timings, draw calls, render-scale and switch-off experiments, a benchmark mode and a copyable report.

Headless checks

A scripted browser drives the game logic step by step: a collision sweep of every lane (29 blocked spots → 0), traffic soak tests, and the round 24 fixes. These prove the logic works, not the feel. Feel is only judged on Marc’s phone.

Round 24 measured (logic only)

  • Straight 250 m in 10.18 s, 90% top speed at 3.5 s, top 61 mph
  • Brake from 61 mph: 11.7 m (a real car needs about 40 m)
  • Head-on at 20.6 m/s with damage off: health stays 100
  • Brake + stick: reverses at 6.2 m/s while turning

How it got here

  1. Start: first brief was a pixel-art Chinatown-style city, then switched to real 3D, with Blender models and a Three.js phone viewer.
  2. Early rounds: scene kit, lighting, a rigged character (idle, walk, punch), modular car doors and enter/exit animations.
  3. Step 2–3: colliders from Blender, arcade car physics and crashes, touch controls; on-foot hero, punch combat (hit-stop, knockback, knockdown), enter any car.
  4. Florida 1–5: moved to Coconut Creek. Vegetation, stucco and terracotta buildings, boulevards, and a data-driven world with minimap, money and health.
  5. City skeleton → plan v5/v6: traced Marc’s maps into map data; rebuilt the whole island from it, with roads, lakes, bridges and landmarks.
  6. Round 19: Lyons Rd made the main road; all 15 vehicle kinds built.
  7. Round 20: road audit, phone performance pass, measurement HUD, traffic AI, pedestrians, police, missions.
  8. Round 21: breakable trees, heavier player car, blood and ragdoll, casino turned to the road, Trash Mountain moved, car polish.
  9. Round 22: joystick default, lane-by-lane collision audit, unstick, warm-up draw, save/restore, HUD and pause-menu cleanup, AI tuning.
  10. Round 23: carjacking, horn, Wasted/Busted respawn, title screen, full map, sound pass.
  11. Round 24 (now): driving research brief adopted. Bug fixes (on-foot auto-run, reverse steering, damage off, silent switch, stuck touches, even foot speed) and tools (all numbers in Tune, smooth drawing, readout, test track).

Keep Lyons Rd, Coconut Creek Pkwy and Wiles Rd. Proposed: Northridge Rd → Sample Rd, South Loop Rd → Copans Rd, Creekview Dr → Winston Park Blvd, West Creek Rd → Hammock Blvd, Townhome Ln → Banks Rd (far west, where Dave’s house goes).

Open questions

Decisions that are Marc’s, and the unknowns the research brief says nobody has measured. Useful input for a design-questions chat.

decide Controls and camera

  • Package A (camera follows the car’s heading) or B (north-up, stick = direction)? A breaks the “always north-up” camera while driving.
  • Auto-gas on by default, or manual pedals?
  • Should reverse ever happen without pressing Brake?
  • How much sliding is fun: grippy arcade, or drifty?
  • Portrait only, or a landscape mode later?

decide Game design

  • What is the core loop once driving feels good: Dave’s quests, free-roam challenges, chases?
  • How do the three playable characters differ beyond their cars (e.g., Aaron’s self-driving Tesla as a mechanic)?
  • Should crashes ever cost anything again (damage, health), or stay speed-only?
  • What does money buy?
  • How dark should the crime side be? (Blood is already a switch.)

unknown Not measured anywhere

  • Screen-relative vs car-relative steering on a phone: no study exists.
  • Portrait vs landscape for driving.
  • Chinatown Wars’ real handling and camera numbers.
  • iPhone touch-to-screen delay, and the visible height with Safari’s bars.

known issues

  • Brakes are very harsh (11.7 m from 61 mph).
  • Steering at mid speed is about twice as sharp as the brief suggests.
  • Turning around with the joystick is awkward (Stage 3).
  • The minimap shows the city while you’re on the test track.
  • Retail Commons west is still mostly a thin strip.
